questiontext.text: What does selection sort do on each iteration?

answer.text: Finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it to the boundary of the sorted part

feedback.text: Correct — it selects the smallest remaining element and places it next.

answer.text: Compares and swaps adjacent elements repeatedly

feedback.text: That describes bubble sort.

answer.text: Shifts larger sorted elements right to insert the next element

feedback.text: That describes insertion sort.

answer.text: Partitions the array around a pivot

feedback.text: That describes quicksort.

generalfeedback.text: Selection sort scans the unsorted region for its minimum, then swaps that minimum into the growing sorted prefix's boundary.

questiontext.text: How many comparisons does selection sort make across best, average, and worst cases?

answer.text: Always Θ(n^2) — it is not adaptive

feedback.text: Correct — it scans the whole unsorted part every time regardless of input order.

answer.text: O(n) in the best case, O(n^2) otherwise

feedback.text: No — unlike insertion or bubble sort, selection sort has no early-exit; it always does Θ(n^2) comparisons.

answer.text: O(n log n) on average

feedback.text: No — selection sort does not divide the problem; it is quadratic.

answer.text: O(n) always

feedback.text: No — finding each minimum requires scanning the remaining elements.

generalfeedback.text: Selection sort always performs about n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of the input, so best = average = worst = Θ(n^2). It is not adaptive.

questiontext.text: What is notable about the number of swaps (writes) selection sort performs?

answer.text: Only O(n) swaps — at most one per iteration

feedback.text: Correct — this makes it attractive when writes are expensive (e.g. flash memory).

answer.text: O(n^2) swaps, matching its comparison count

feedback.text: No — comparisons are O(n^2) but swaps are only O(n).

answer.text: O(n log n) swaps

feedback.text: No — selection sort does at most one swap per pass, so O(n) total.

answer.text: Zero swaps; it uses an auxiliary array

feedback.text: No — it sorts in place with swaps.

generalfeedback.text: Selection sort makes at most one swap per outer iteration, so only O(n) writes overall — useful when write cost dominates.

questiontext.text: The standard array-based selection sort is a stable sorting algorithm.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: No — swapping a distant minimum into place can jump one equal key past another, breaking relative order.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — the standard array version is not stable.

questiontext.text: Selection sort is in-place, using only O(1) extra space.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — it sorts by swapping within the array, needing only constant extra memory.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Selection sort needs no auxiliary array; swaps happen in place.

questiontext.text: On each pass, selection sort searches the unsorted part for its ______ element (the smallest). Answer in one English word.

answer.text: minimum

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: minimum*

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: min*

feedback.text: Correct — "minimum".

answer.text: smallest

feedback.text: Correct — the minimum element.

questiontext.text: Which statements about selection sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It performs only O(n) swaps, useful when writes are costly

feedback.text: Yes — at most one swap per outer pass.

answer.text: Its comparison count is Θ(n^2) regardless of the input

feedback.text: Yes — it is not adaptive.

answer.text: It runs in O(n) on an already-sorted array

feedback.text: No — it is not adaptive; it is always Θ(n^2) comparisons.

answer.text: The standard array version is stable

feedback.text: No — the standard array version is not stable.

generalfeedback.text: Selection sort: always Θ(n^2) comparisons but only O(n) swaps; in-place; not adaptive; the standard array version is not stable.

questiontext.text: When is selection sort a particularly reasonable choice?

answer.text: When the cost of writing/swapping elements dominates and you want to minimize the number of writes

feedback.text: Correct — it does at most O(n) swaps, which is its main practical appeal.

answer.text: When the input is nearly sorted and you want O(n) behaviour

feedback.text: No — selection sort is not adaptive; insertion sort is the adaptive choice.

answer.text: When you must sort millions of records quickly

feedback.text: No — O(n^2) comparisons make it too slow at scale.

generalfeedback.text: Selection sort's edge is its O(n) writes; choose it when swaps/writes are the expensive operation, not for large or nearly-sorted inputs.
